svg.text: The register sees fishing fleets, not fish farms.
anyone using a record count as a proxy for how well a species
whether a species is under-observed for how widely it is met
a longer farmed list separates from the background, making the
records against the number of datasets reporting the species
1,143 species from five classes, sampled across the record range
Wild-capture species sit a full standard deviation above the line and farmed
species sit on it. A farmed oyster never enters a trawl survey, so
aquaculture is invisible here and no model will recover it. The forty
largest residuals contain none of the declared species — they are one-survey
species with a median of 13 datasets against the declared list's 105, so the
commercial signal is a shift in the middle, not a tail. Only a list written
species in 40+ datasets with the largest shortfall against the fit
These are met by forty or more separate programmes and counted a fraction of
what that breadth implies. It is a research-attention list that needs
nobody's opinion of what matters. Among species in 40+ datasets, the
over-counted are more often IUCN-threatened than the under-counted, 21.4%
against 8.1% — the same direction as figure 11, on nine species against
five, so it is a hint and not a finding.
OBIS v3 checklist and /dataset, fetched 2026-09-19. Breadth is the count of datasets reporting the species; /v3/node takes a scientificname and
returns 39 for everything, which is the total node count, so it cannot be used. Species were drawn stratified by log10(records) from five classes,
seed 20260919, with every declared control added regardless of the draw. Checklists are paged with skip because the endpoint caps at 10,000 and sorts
by record count — the variable being modelled. p-values are two-sided permutation tests on the median, 20,000 draws, against the 1,093 unlabelled
